turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Indeed, Mr. Darcy? I am quite intrigued to hear your 'contemptuous' assessment of a gentleman whose misfortunes you seem so eager to belittle. Pray, enlighten me: what precisely are these 'great misfortunes' you speak of, and what role, may I ask, have *you* played in their creation?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You presume, Miss Bennet, to demand an explanation of Mr. Wickham’s history from me, as if I were bound to offer it! It is a history replete with deceit and manipulation, and one which, I assure you, is far less flattering than your sentimentality allows. I will not indulge your misguided sympathy for a man who has proven himself wholly unworthy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So, Mr. Darcy, it appears I have offended you by exhibiting a degree of compassion? I find it remarkably convenient that you only deign to enlighten me on Mr. Wickham’s character *after* I’ve expressed some sympathy. Tell me, is your purpose truly to defend Mr. Wickham's reputation, or merely to demonstrate your own superior knowledge?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: My purpose, Miss Bennet, is not to demonstrate superiority, though it appears that is a consequence you find difficult to comprehend. I merely observe that your affections are easily swayed by charming falsehoods, and I am compelled to defend truth, even when it is unwelcome to those who prefer pleasant illusions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Defend truth, you say? How very noble of you, Mr. Darcy. I daresay it is a convenient banner to hide behind when attempting to discredit anyone who dares question your actions or motives.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are tiresome and, frankly, unwarranted. I assure you, my actions are guided by a sense of responsibility and a desire to protect those vulnerable to manipulation, not by a wish to discredit anyone who dares to possess an independent mind. I find myself increasingly compelled to question the wisdom of this conversation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Responsibility? Is that what you call it, Mr. Darcy? It sounds remarkably like self-righteousness to me, a convenient cloak for your interference and, I suspect, a great deal of vanity. Pray tell, what vulnerability required *your* protection?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your relentless pursuit of finding fault in my character is both tiresome and, I confess, rather bewildering. I speak of my actions regarding Mr. Wickham and Miss King, not to boast, but to illuminate the depths of his deceit – a deceit you, in your haste to judge, appear entirely willing to overlook. It is a vulnerability of innocence, Miss Bennet, that I deemed worthy of protection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Oh, Wickham and Miss King, is it? How very convenient that your 'protection' serves to absolve yourself of any responsibility for the consequences of your meddling. I daresay if you had left well enough alone, a great deal of unpleasantness might have been avoided.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistent misinterpretations are becoming exceedingly difficult to endure. I did not seek to absolve myself of responsibility, but rather to prevent further damage stemming from Mr. Wickham’s deplorable character – a character you, with your evident partiality, seem determined to defend.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Partiality? Really, Mr. Darcy? My only failing, as you so generously point out, is the audacity to form my own opinions without consulting the superior judgment of a gentleman who believes himself entitled to dictate the lives of others. I find your accusations rather tiresome, even when draped in such an elaborate display of wounded dignity.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your words are designed to inflict pain, and whilst I may find them tiresome, I will not allow them to diminish the sincerity of my sentiments. My intentions, however misguided you may believe them, are rooted in a deep and abiding regard for your happiness – a regard which, I confess, transcends the constraints of propriety and reason. I am, plainly, in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? You declare your love after a relentless campaign of interference and condescension? It is a most extraordinary proposal, Mr. Darcy, and I confess, I find it almost as bewildering as your previous attempts to justify your behaviour.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am not entirely surprised by your incredulity; my actions have, I concede, been poorly explained. However, to suggest I have engaged in a 'campaign of interference' is a gross misrepresentation of my efforts to protect those I hold dear, and, dare I say, to shield *you* from the consequences of imprudence.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Shield me from imprudence? Is that what you call preventing Jane from accepting a most amiable gentleman, and then attempting to smear Mr. Wickham’s name with accusations that, conveniently, serve *your* purposes? I daresay you believe yourself a benevolent protector, but your actions reek of arrogance and control.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations, whilst delivered with a certain… vivacity, are profoundly unfair. Mr. Wickham’s character is beyond redemption, a truth you seem determined to ignore, and my actions regarding Miss Jane Bennet were motivated solely by a desire to prevent a union founded upon precarious affections. I will not apologize for acting with what I believe to be prudence and good sense.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Prudence and good sense? You presume to lecture me on such virtues while dismantling the happiness of others? I find it remarkably convenient that your 'prudence' always seems to align with the preservation of your own family’s reputation, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your observations are laced with a regrettable degree of… conjecture. While I acknowledge the perception that my actions are often dictated by a concern for my family's standing, I assure you that my intentions, however clumsily manifested, are rooted in a desire for what I deem to be the greatest good for all involved.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: The 'greatest good,' you say? It appears your definition of goodness involves manipulating the lives of others and then justifying it with lofty pronouncements. I am quite familiar with self-deception, Mr. Darcy, and you, it seems, are a master of the art.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your accusations increasingly tiresome. It is a grave injustice to suggest I derive pleasure from manipulating the lives of others; I assure you, the burdens of responsibility which accompany my station are often far heavier than you can possibly comprehend.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
